analysis.one_liner: Lets regulators and courts crack down harder on dominant companies that crush competitors.
analysis.headline: Introduced by three Democratic senators, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it easier to prove that a dominant company has broken antitrust law. Any company with more than half of a market would be presumed to be acting illegally if it takes actions that hurt competitors, unless it can show the conduct actually helps competition. It would also let the Justice Department and the Federal Trade Commission impose much larger fines — up to 15 percent of a company's total U.S. revenue — and would stop courts from shielding regulated industries from antitrust suits. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers facing higher prices, workers facing lower wages from employer concentration, and small businesses that compete against dominant firms would gain if enforcement got easier and penalties got bigger.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes conduct that materially disadvantages or forecloses competitors unlawful, and creates a presumption that it is illegal when done by a firm with more than 50 percent market share or significant market power, unless the firm proves the conduct produces real competitive benefits [S3].

It authorizes civil penalties of up to the greater of 15 percent of a company's total U.S. revenues from the previous year, or 30 percent of its U.S. revenues in the affected line of commerce, enforceable by the Attorney General and the FTC [S3].
It says courts cannot require proving a defined market when there is direct evidence of harm to competition, removing a technical hurdle that often defeats antitrust cases [S3].
It limits courts' ability to imply immunity from antitrust laws for conduct regulated by federal agencies, and directs DOJ and FTC to issue joint enforcement guidelines with public comment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Dominant firms — companies with more than half of a market or significant market power — would face presumption of liability and potential fines in the billions, plus higher litigation exposure and compliance costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Dominant firms with big market shares

drawbacks.text: The presumption attaches to any conduct that disadvantages competitors by any firm above 50 percent market share, which could capture aggressive but legitimate competition — like steep discounting or rapid product improvement — and deter it, because the bill expressly says below-cost pricing is not required to prove a violation [S3].

Penalties of 15 percent of total U.S. revenues are vastly larger than existing antitrust fines and could be disproportionate for a single violation, raising the risk of settlement-pressure on large firms regardless of the merits [S3].

Businesses would face uncertainty under a new, broader standard of liability applied with less need for market definition, which supporters see as necessary flexibility and critics see as unpredictable legal exposure [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers and workers, the upside is a long-overdue tightening of antitrust enforcement against dominant firms whose conduct the current, court-built standards often excuse. The costs fall on large firms in the form of penalties and litigation risk, though the breadth of the presumption could also chill some genuinely procompetitive behavior. The bill died before any of this could be weighed in committee or on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the Anticompetitive Exclusionary Conduct Prevention Act of 2020 on March 10, 2020, joined by Sens. Richard Blumenthal and Cory Booker [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — was taken for the remainder of the 116th Congress, which ended January 3, 2021 [S5].
The bill carried 2 cosponsors, both Democrats, and no Republican support [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Dominant firms with large market shares are better off, because the stricter liability standard and revenue-based penalties never took effect, and antitrust enforcement remained under the more permissive court doctrines the bill sought to change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Dominant firms that avoided stricter antitrust rules

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to tighten antitrust liability for dominant firms and increase enforcement penalties.

for.name: Sens. Richard Blumenthal and Cory Booker
for.role: U.S. Senators from Connecticut and New Jersey
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original co-sponsors.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All three Senate supporters were Democrats and the bill drew no Republican cosponsors; it never advanced far enough to produce a vote that would show the broader partisan split.

industries.industry: Dominant firms with large market shares (including large tech platforms, retailers, and other near-monopolies)
industries.note: The bill would have presumed any conduct disadvantaging competitors to be illegal for firms above 50 percent market share, with fines up to 15 percent of total U.S. revenues. Those firms gain when such enforcement never happens, at the expense of the higher prices and fewer choices the bill's findings attribute to concentrated market power [S3].

The bill would give small competitors an easier path to sue firms that exclude or foreclose them, without first proving a defined market. They benefit only if such a law passes, which this one did not [S3].
